doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

title: How Eastman study changed his improvising
summary: He wants to be an informed ear player and says melody can trump the changes when he goes against the grain.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Okay. Yeah, you had said, I had read something about you liked to go off with your mistakes, so I got a whole CD of your mistakes we’ll listen to — just kidding.

I’m going to backtrack a little bit. You talked about when you got to Eastman you needed to bone up on your theory some, and get more informed about that. Do you think it changed the way you improvised?

Yes, I feel it’s continuing to. I just, I sort of consider myself an ear player to a degree, but I want to be an informed ear player. I mean so I know the changes of songs, and I don’t play tunes I don’t know, and I know a lot of songs. And I can play piano well enough to comp for my students. So my colleagues are very informed, like Bill Dobbins, and Harold, and Dariusz and Jeff. Jeff is the bass teacher. But they’re very informed. I’m sort of probably the loose cannon of the bunch in terms of theory. I’m not quite as literal as them maybe. But piano players maybe are more literal. I don’t know. But they’re all different too, all three of those guys. But my ears got better I think, having been at Eastman for 16 years. And I’ve decided I’m paying more close attention to details, especially when I’m practicing. And then when I go to play I think it comes out better. Even though I go against the grain harmonically quite a lot. I do think it’s better for me to know those details better.

When you go against the grain, which I like that term, do you make a specific choice, what’s that going to be? I’m not sure I can be specific about it. If it’s a C9 chord are there formulas to go against the grain with that?

Yes, to a degree. But mine’s more — a little bit more serendipitous. To me it’s not chord by chord, it’s more contextual. Like I tell my students, and I try to be myself too, is more compositional improvisationally. So using the melody of the tune might steer me in a different way musically than following the changes per se, and it might go against the grain that way. And to me the melody kind of trumps the changes at that point. So some people might not agree with that. I’m sure they don’t. Some people may think that I’m not following them close enough. So I definitely — it’s all relative. Because sometimes people have said to me, like when I used to do recording sessions in Los Angeles people would say, “this needs to be like right down the middle.” And I’d play what I thought was right down the middle and they’d say, “well that’s not what we were looking for.”
This was on people’s jazz dates?
